justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modestly bullish near-term bias with a fairly flat trajectory across horizons. For the 1-day estimate, I anchored close to recent price action, assuming no major overnight catalyst would dramatically shift the level. The 1-week estimate nudges slightly higher, reflecting a mild continuation of whatever near-term momentum exists, while the 1-month estimate edges a bit further up, incorporating a small positive drift assumption consistent with longer-run equity market tendencies. The flatness across all three horizons signals that I did not have strong conviction about a directional move — rather, I expected mean-reverting behavior around a stable central tendency.

The confidence interval widths were calibrated to typical realized volatility at each time horizon, scaled roughly by the square root of time. For a single day, the range is tight because most daily moves fall within a predictable band absent a major shock. Over a week, more trading sessions accumulate, and macro data releases, Fed speakers, or earnings surprises can compound, so the band widens accordingly. Over a month, the interval spans roughly 36 points (176 to 212), reflecting that a full month introduces substantial uncertainty from earnings cycles, economic data revisions, geopolitical developments, and shifts in market sentiment that simply cannot be anticipated at the time of forecasting.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside the stated intervals include a surprise Federal Reserve policy shift — either an unexpected rate cut or a hawkish pivot — which could easily move markets by more than my stated ranges capture. A significant geopolitical escalation, a major credit event, or an unexpected shock to labor market or inflation data could similarly produce a tail move. On the upside, a stronger-than-expected resolution to trade tensions or a better-than-anticipated earnings season could drive prices well above 212 over the month horizon.

It is also worth acknowledging that my intervals may be somewhat narrow given the current macro environment. Elevated policy uncertainty and shifting rate expectations tend to fatten the tails of return distributions beyond what historical volatility alone would suggest. If implied volatility were elevated at the time of the forecast, a prudent adjustment would have been to widen the confidence intervals, particularly at the 1-month horizon, to more honestly reflect the probability mass sitting in the tails.
